Acitretin has been shown to reduce the contraceptive efficacy of norethindrone-based preparations. 3. A family history of breast cancer, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or pulmonary embolism (PE), as well as a personal or past history of depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), changes in bone mineral density, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), should be carefully considered when prescribing oral contraceptives. 4. Conditions that may worsen due to fluid retention, such as migraines, asthma, or epilepsy, should also be taken into account. 5. Therapy should be discontinued if jaundice, visual disturbances (which may lead to contact lens intolerance), signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE), unusually severe migraines, significant increases in blood pressure, severe depression, or an increased risk of thromboembolic complications following surgery develop. 6. Women with a history of depression should be closely monitored, and therapy should be discontinued if depression recurs to a severe degree. 7. Oral contraceptives should be discontinued at least four weeks prior to major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 8. Patients on warfarin or other oral anticoagulants may require an increased dose of anticoagulants when using oral contraceptives. 9. There is an increased risk of cervical cancer associated with oral contraceptive use, particularly with long-term use (five or more years), although human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor for this cancer. 10. Oral contraceptive use has been linked to an increased risk of liver cancer, with the risk rising with longer durations of use. 11. Some studies suggest an association between oral contraceptive use and an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in certain populations. 12. Benign hepatic adenomas have been associated with oral contraceptive use, although their incidence is rare in the United States. 13. In women with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may induce or exacerbate symptoms of angioedema. 14. The CDC recommends waiting at least three weeks after vaginal delivery or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives to reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism. Women with additional risk factors for VTE should avoid combined hormonal contraceptives altogether. 15. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. Additionally, there is no evidence of teratogenic effects, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when oral contraceptives are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. 16. Oral contraceptives should not be used to induce withdrawal bleeding as a test for pregnancy, nor should they be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. 17. If a patient misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing oral contraceptive use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, pregnancy should be considered at the time of the first missed period. Oral contraceptives should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. 18. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been identified in the breast milk of nursing mothers, with a few adverse effects on the child reported, including jaundice and breast enlargement. 19. Oral contraceptives administered during the postpartum period may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. 20. Ethinyl estradiol reduces the release of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) from the hypothalamus and gonadotropin release from the pituitary. It also increases the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and various proteins in target tissues. 21. Norethindrone acetate, a progestin, inhibits the secretion of gonadotropins from the pituitary, prevents follicular maturation and ovulation, and stimulates the growth of mammary tissues. 22. The peak plasma time for ethinyl estradiol is approximately eight hours, while for norethindrone, it is one to two hours. 23. Ethinyl estradiol has a volume of distribution (Vd) of 2-4 L/kg and is 80% protein-bound, while norethindrone is 61% protein-bound. Both components are metabolized in the liver, with ethinyl estradiol undergoing extensive first-pass metabolism. 24. The metabolites of ethinyl estradiol include estriol and estrone, while norethindrone metabolites include sulfate and glucuronide conjugates, which are inactive. 25. The half-life of ethinyl estradiol when taken orally is approximately 19-24 hours. 26. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only.
